source_text:
[ἐν δὲ] ἔσονται οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι.«
Ταῦτα μὲν ἐν τῷ κατὰ Μάρκον εὐαγγελίῳ γέγραπται· καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἄλλοις δὲ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἀνωμολογημένοις ὀλίγον μὲν ἴσως ἑκασταχοῦ τῶν ῥημάτων ἐναλλάσσει, πάντα δὲ τὴν αὐτὴν τῆς γνώμης συμφωνίαν ἐπιδείκνυται. δεὶ δὲ σαφῶς εἰδότας ὡς οὐδὲν ἀνθρωπίνως ὁ σωτήρ. ἀλλὰ πάντα θείᾳ σοφίᾳ καὶ μυστικῇ διδάσκει τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ, μὴ σαρκίνως ἀκροᾶσθαι τῶν λεγομένων. ἀλλὰ τὸν ἐν αὐτοῖς κεκρυμμένον νοῦν μετὰ τῆς ἀξίας ζητήσεως καὶ συνέσεως ἐρευνᾶν καὶ καταμανθάνειν. καὶ γὰρ τὰ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ τοῦ κυρίου δοκοῦντα ἡπλῶσθαι πρὸς τοὺς μαθητὰς τῶν ᾐνιγμένως ὑπειρημένων οὐδὲν ἥττονος [ἔτι καὶ νῦν]. ἀλλὰ πλείονος ἔτι καὶ νῦν τῆς ἐπιστάσεως εὑρίσκεται δεόμενα διὰ τὴν ὑπερβάλλουσαν τῆς φρονήσεως ἐν αὐτοῖς ὑπερβολήν. ὅπου δὲ καὶ τὰ νομιζόμενα ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ διοῖχθαι τοῖς ἔσω καὶ αὐτοῖς τοῖς τῆς βασιλείας τέκνοις ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ καλουμένοις ἔτι χρῄζει φροντίδος πλείονος, ἦ πού γε τὰ δόξαντα μὲν ἁπλῶς ἐξενηνέχθαι καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μηδὲ διηρωτημένα πρὸς τῶν ἀκουσάντων, εἰς ὅλον δὲ τὸ τέλος αὐτὸ τῆς σωτηρίας διαφέροντα. ἐσκεπασμένα δὲ θαυμαστῷ καὶ ὑπερουρανίῳ διανοίας βάθει, οὐκ ἐπιπολαίως δέχεσθαι ταῖς ἀκοαῖς προσῆκεν, ἀλλὰ καθιέντας τὸν νοῦν ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ σωτῆρος καὶ τὸ τῆς γνώμης ἀπόρρητον.
thought_title: The hidden depth of the Savior's words
orientation: Clement has just quoted the Gospel dialogue about the rich man and now explains how the Savior's words must be read.
pass_a_gloss: But the first will be last and the last first. These things have been written in the Gospel according to Mark; and in all the other acknowledged Gospels, each perhaps changes the wording a little here and there, but all display the same agreement of meaning. But it is necessary that those who know clearly that the Savior teaches nothing in a merely human way, but teaches all things to his own by divine and mystical wisdom, should not listen to the things said in a fleshly way, but should search out and learn the hidden mind in them with worthy seeking and understanding. For even the things that seem to have been spoken simply by the Lord himself to the disciples are found to require no less attention even now than the things spoken in riddles, but even more attention even now, because of the surpassing excess of wisdom in them. And where even the things thought to have been opened by him to those within, to those very ones called by him children of the kingdom, still need more care, how much more the things that seemed to have been uttered simply and for this reason were not even questioned by the hearers, but that bear on the whole end of salvation itself. And being covered with a wondrous and supercelestial depth of thought, it was not fitting to receive them superficially with the ears, but to send the mind down to the very spirit of the Savior and the secret of his meaning.

choices.why: Refers to the Gospels universally recognized by the church; 'acknowledged' preserves the sense of common confession rather than a modern canonical term.

choices.english: should not listen in a fleshly way
choices.why: The adverb σαρκίνως contrasts fleshly hearing with spiritual understanding; 'fleshly' keeps the Pauline and Clementine sense of merely human or carnal perception.
νοῦς here means the deeper meaning or intent hidden in the words; 'mind' preserves the intellectual-spiritual sense Clement intends.
ἐπίστασις means close application or scrutiny; 'attention' fits the context of careful study required for the Savior's words.

choices.term: ὑπερβάλλουσαν τῆς φρονήσεως ἐν αὐτοῖς ὑπερβολήν
choices.english: the surpassing excess of wisdom in them
choices.why: The double use of ὑπερβάλλω and ὑπερβολή is emphatic; rendering both as 'surpassing excess' preserves the rhetorical force.
καθίημι means to let down or send down; the image is of lowering the mind into the depth of the Savior's spirit, which 'sending the mind down' captures literally.

bible_refs.note: ἔσονται οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι

pass_b_english: “But the first will be last, and the last first” (Mark 10:31).
This is what is written in the Gospel according to Mark. And in all the other acknowledged Gospels, the wording may vary a little here and there, but they all display the same agreement of meaning.

We must know clearly that the Savior does nothing in a merely human way, but everything by divine and mystical wisdom. So we should not listen to his words in a fleshly way, but search out and thoroughly learn the hidden mind in them with the worthy inquiry and understanding they deserve.
For even the things the Lord himself seems to have spoken simply to his disciples are found to require no less attention now—indeed, even more—because of the surpassing excess of wisdom in them.

And where even the things thought to have been opened by him to those within, to those called children of the kingdom, still need greater care, how much more do the things that seemed to be spoken simply and were therefore not even questioned by his hearers, yet bear on the whole end of salvation itself?

These are veiled in a wondrous and supercelestial depth of thought, and it is not fitting to receive them superficially with the ears, but by sending the mind down to the very Spirit of the Savior and the secret of his purpose.

problems.quote: But many who are first will be last, and the last first” (Mark 10:31).
problems.source_quote: ἔσονται οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι.
problems.why: Greek does not contain ‘many’; Clement’s text says simply ‘the first will be last, and the last first’. Adding ‘many’ changes the meaning.
problems.fix: But the first will be last, and the last first” (Mark 10:31).
problems.ruling: Greek lacks 'many' (πολλοὶ); adding it changes Clement's quoted text, misrepresenting his biblical citation.

problems.quote: the Savior teaches his own nothing in a merely human way
problems.why: Greek means ‘the Savior does nothing in a human way’; English adds ‘teaches his own nothing’, misrepresenting the verb and meaning.
problems.fix: the Savior does nothing in a merely human way
problems.ruling: ὁ σωτὴρ is subject of οὐδὲν ἀνθρωπίνως with implied verb; 'does nothing humanly' not 'teaches his own nothing'.
